concept: Ocean waves result from the superposition of waves generated by wind on the water surface. Wave height, period, and direction depend on wind speed, duration of the event, and fetch distance (generation area).
analogy: Imagine throwing stones into a pond: each stone creates circular waves that interfere with others. In the ocean, millions of 'stones' (wind gusts) create a complex interference pattern.
real_world_example: The Pacific Ocean shows waves of ~15m significant height during storms, with periods of 12-15 seconds. Swell propagates thousands of kilometers to distant coasts.
references: Kinsman, B. (1965). Wind Waves: Their Generation and Propagation on the Ocean Surface
Holthuijsen, L.H. (2007). Waves in Oceanic and Coastal Waters

algorithmic.why_this_algorithm: Simplex Noise eliminates the visible directional artifacts of classic Perlin Noise by using a simplex grid instead of square. It's faster in higher dimensions and produces smoother gradients.

comparison.advantage: No directional artifacts, faster in high dimension
